newsitem.title: JAPAN: Sterling down, dollar/yen steady by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Sterling down, dollar/yen steady by late Tokyo.

text.p: The British pound fell across board in late Tokyo trading partly in reaction to a British newspaper column suggesting that the Labour party may like to take a soft pound policy, dealers said.
The pound fell to around $1.6175 after triggering stop-loss sales near $1.62, while it also fell to near 2.7855 marks by late Tokyo.

"The article sparked heavy loss-cut sales by interbank traders in Tokyo as well as by overseas accounts," a chief dealer at a Japanese long-term bank said. Other dealers said the article also led to long-liquidation sales in sterling.

A dealer at British bank said traders took that article to mean that the victorious Labour party will need to see a softer pound in the near future in order to avoid a sharp drop in the currency if Britain eventually joins European economic and monetary union.
By 0640 GMT, the British pound fell to around $1.6120, compared with $1.6235/45 at Thursday's New York close.

"Although the British economy is in good shape, the report raised speculation that Britain may try to reduce the burden of its strong currency on the economy," said a senior dealer at a French bank in Tokyo. A weaker currency would make a nation's exporters more competitive abroad.

Dealers said the Labour party's landslide victory in the British general election in itself did not have much impact on the Tokyo market, but they added that they would continue to focus on potential policy changes, particularly in regards to European monetary union and the chance of an interest rate rise.
A dealer with a U.S. bank said: "Most of the pound sales came from London, while Tokyo traders unloaded some long sterling positions along the way."
Markets are now focused on a monetary meeting between the finance minister and Bank of England Governor Eddie George scheduled for May 7, which could well result in a small rise in interest rates.

The greenback remained steady against the yen for most of the Asian session, with activity somewhat subdued as traders awaited the release of key U.S. April unemployment data due out at 1230 GMT, dealers said.

Economists expected the April jobless rate to hold steady at 5.2 percent, the average work week to shrink to 34.7 hours in April from 34.8 hours in March and average hourly earnings to rise 0.3 percent after increasing 0.4 percent in March.
Dealers said strong data would increase expectations of a possible rise in U.S. interest rates, which would spark dollar buying for the yen and mark.
The dollar rose as high as 126.93 yen after setting off stop-loss buying near 126.80 yen in thin trade in the afternoon, but its gains were capped by sales, possibly by U.S. operators.

In addition, the dollar's topside remained heavy amid lingering concern about possible dollar-sales intervention, particularly after the dollar fell overnight due to rumours of looming intervention, dealers said.
